strengths: Novel problem formulation investigating mismatch between traditional complexity metrics and LLM-perceived difficulty, with valuable empirical finding that traditional metrics lose correlation once code length is controlled
Strong and consistent empirical correlations (r = -0.92 to -0.97) across three diverse code-related tasks (program repair, code translation, execution reasoning)
Causal validation through semantics-preserving code rewriting experiments showing up to 20.9% performance improvements while constraining cyclomatic complexity
Solid theoretical framework with rigorous proofs (Theorem 3.3 on hierarchical entropy accumulation) and clear assumptions grounded in recent LLM literature
Well-motivated metric design capturing complementary dimensions of semantic complexity (compositional depth and branching-induced divergence) through entropy-guided hierarchical decomposition
Methodologically sound experiments using proper statistical controls (partial correlations, subgroup-based analysis) and rigorous ablation studies
weaknesses: Critical concern: Entropy computation uses CodeLlama-7B-HF but metric is evaluated with DeepSeek-V3, creating an unvalidated cross-model transfer that undermines claims about LLM-perceived complexity; entropy threshold τ=0.67 from prior work may not be optimal for different models

Severely limited evaluation scope reduces generalizability: only Python (no other languages), only 3 code tasks, only 1 primary LLM (DeepSeek-V3), small filtered datasets (271-535 samples), and no evaluation on other major models (GPT-4, Claude, Llama)

Task-specific sensitivity undermines universality claims: Table 2 shows different features correlate best with different tasks; Figure 3 shows α must be tuned per-task for optimal performance, suggesting the metric is not truly universal

Missing critical baselines and ablations: no comparison with simpler alternatives (code length alone, nesting depth, raw structural metrics); no validation that LM-CC captures more than residual length effects; no ablation on entropy vs. structural segmentation components

Limited failure analysis: no investigation of code types where metric performs poorly; no discussion of failure modes; rewriting experiment introduces selection bias by only retaining successful rewrites
Computational cost not addressed: requires CodeLlama-7B inference for every code sample, with no discussion of practical deployment, approximations, or cost-performance tradeoffs

strengths: Novel problem identification: First systematic study demonstrating that traditional code complexity metrics fail to correlate with LLM performance; timely and important contribution

Rigorous empirical methodology: Proper use of partial correlation analysis controlling for length, subgroup-based correlation analysis across multiple tasks, and both correlational and causal validation approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Consistent results across 4 code tasks, 6+ LLM variants, 4 entropy models, with detailed ablation studies (Table 5, Figure 3) demonstrating robustness
Theoretical grounding: Theorem 3.3 on hierarchical entropy accumulation and Proposition B.1 elegantly showing Θ(n) vs Θ(n²) separation from cyclomatic complexity explain why traditional metrics fail
Practical utility demonstrated: Code rewriting experiments show meaningful improvements up to 20.9% with semantics preserved and traditional complexity held constant

Strong correlations: LM-CC achieves -0.80 to -0.97 partial correlations across tasks, substantially outperforming traditional metrics and showing consistent statistical significance across all 16 settings
weaknesses: Potential circular dependency with entropy-based evaluation: LM-CC uses token-level entropy from pretrained models to decompose code, but task-performing models may be different families. While results span entropy models, the fundamental concern that entropy signals capture model-family-specific rather than universal LLM difficulty isn't adequately addressed

Limited justification for metric design: Why weighted sum (Eq. 4) over other aggregation strategies? Feature selection based on post-hoc coverage analysis (14/16, 13/16) rather than principled approach. Task-dependent α selection (Figure 3) raises generalization questions for practitioners

Code rewriting experiments have limited scope: Only 58-99 valid rewrites per task, introducing selection bias. Keeping CC constant may not isolate LM-CC's causal effect if metrics capture orthogonal aspects. DeepSeek-V3.2 rewriting introduces potential confounds

Entropy threshold sensitivity not adequately analyzed: τ=0.67 set 'following prior work' without systematic sensitivity analysis. Proposition B.3's bimodal assumption isn't empirically validated in the paper. Critical since semantic boundaries drive all downstream calculations

Significant computational cost limits practical adoption: 0.02-0.7 s/sample vs 0.1-0.9 ms for cyclomatic complexity (20-7000x slowdown). Should be discussed more prominently as fundamental barrier to deployment

Generalization limitations: Evaluation limited to Python code; applicability to other languages unclear. Code tasks narrow (repair, translation, execution reasoning). Theoretical assumptions (context degradation, branching uncertainty) motivated by citations but not directly validated on evaluated models

Theoretical assumptions not empirically validated: Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 rely on cited findings but aren't verified in this paper's experimental setup. Bounds are acknowledged as conservative and don't capture full depth-branching interactions

Length control interpretation ambiguous: Alternative interpretation—code length dominates LLM difficulty, so traditional metrics' failure when controlled for length may be expected rather than surprising. More nuanced discussion needed

Statistical issues: Multiple comparison problem with reporting 'largest correlation' across 9-11 groupings without multiplicity correction. Execution reasoning at 94.1% baseline introduces ceiling effects limiting effectiveness demonstration

strengths: Well-motivated research question with convincing empirical demonstration that traditional complexity metrics fail to predict LLM performance; partial correlation analysis properly controls for code length confounds
Novel and intuitive technical approach using token-level entropy to drive hierarchical semantic decomposition, capturing compositional depth and branching-induced semantic divergence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 LLM models and 4 diverse tasks with strong consistent correlations (r = -0.80 to -0.97) and careful ablation studies validating design choices
Causal intervention experiments using semantics-preserving code rewriting demonstrate practical utility with significant performance gains (up to 20.9%) while holding cyclomatic complexity constant
Theoretical grounding through Theorem 3.3 on hierarchical entropy accumulation and Proposition B.1 establishing formal separation from cyclomatic complexity
Reproducible methodology with detailed algorithms, extensive experimental protocols, and promised code release; well-written presentation with comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited to Python code and Python-based language models; hierarchical decomposition uses Python-specific indentation structure, raising questions about generalization to other programming languages with different semantic organizations

Entropy threshold τ=0.67 insufficiently justified beyond prior work; no sensitivity analysis provided despite theoretical bimodal assumption not being empirically validated for code; unclear robustness to τ variations

Weighting factor α requires task-specific tuning with significant sensitivity variation (Figure 3 shows sharp performance drops for program repair); no principled guidance for selecting α on novel tasks

Code rewriting experiment has selection bias (only 21-37% valid rewrites) and potential confounds: rewriting prompt requests 'improve comprehensibility' which may reduce complexity beyond LM-CC metric constraints; unclear whether improvements come from metric optimization or human readability enhancement
Computational cost of 0.02-0.7s per sample (100-1000× slower than traditional metrics) limits practical applicability; trade-off between expressiveness and efficiency not adequately addressed

Entropy model selection remains ambiguous with substantial performance variation across models (Table 2); paper suggests larger models are better but provides no clear guidance for practitioners; creates practical dependency undermining 'model-aware' positioning

Theoretical assumptions (3.1-3.2) are empirically motivated but not rigorously derived; 'lost in the middle' and attention sink phenomena may not directly apply to hierarchical code understanding; constructed examples in Proposition B.1 lack empirical validation on natural code

Missing failure analysis: no discussion of when LM-CC fails, edge cases where hierarchical decomposition breaks down, or explanation of non-significant correlations in Table 2; limited to Python and specific model families
